newsitem.title: USA: Dollar stretches gains in U.S. as mark quakes.
newsitem.headline: Dollar stretches gains in U.S. as mark quakes.

text.p: The dollar ended modestly higher in the U.S. after a late session spike to a 33-month peak in dollar/mark fizzled as quickly as it had begun.
The greenback had crept higher throughout the session after surging against the mark overnight on talk of a disappointing federal budget deficit in Germany.

But shortly after noon time in New York the dollar pushed above 1.68 marks for the first time since May 1994. A story on Market News Service Inc. cited an unnamed source familiar with German finance officials saying they would welcome a dollar rally to a range of 1.70 to 1.75 marks.

"The market earlier thought there might be official (German) dollar selling taking place. On the back of the Market News story, the market recognized there were no offers capping the market," said Audrey McNiff, vice president for foreign exchange sales at Goldman Sachs.
But the U.S. unit quickly surrendered those late gains as investors questioned the veracity of the anonymous report.

"The Market News story seemed a little far-fetched. The dollar went screaming up there (to 1.68 marks), but then turned in its tracks," said Kevin Lawrie, head of global foreign exchange at Mellon Bank in Pittsburgh.
The dollar rose to 1.6768/78 marks, up from 1.6720/25 at the open and 1.4370/80 Swiss francs, up from 1.4330/35.
The British pound fell to $1.6365/75 from $1.6410/15 at the open. The dollar rose to 123.25/35 yen from 123.05/15.
Traders said stop-loss buying was triggered after the dollar breached 1.6760 marks, but a large Asian seller near 1.6810 abruptly halted the rally.
The mark slumped against a wide range of currencies, helping boost the dollar against the mark in early trade.
Sterling/mark hit a 52-month high after British radio said Germany's 1997 budget deficit would reach 3.5 percent.
That would exceed the 3.0 percent of gross domestic product threshold for joining a proposed single European currency in 1999.
The pound also rose on a comment from Bank of England deputy Governor Howard Davies, who called for an increase in official British interest rates to guard against inflation.

Germany's troubled economy, struggling with the highest unemployment since before World War II, pales in comparison to the steadily-growing U.S. economy. Investors have flocked to U.S. assets and the dollar as a result, dealers said.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin reinforced that thinking with comments to the House Ways and Means Committee. Rubin said the strong dollar had contributed to a healthy U.S. economy and kept interest rates low.

"The dollar is probably going to go higher. There is good economic fundamental support for the dollar," said Robert Nelson, managing director for foreign exchange sales at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale in New York.
Yet the relatively modest dollar rally on the yen showed investors believe monetary authorities will act to undermine the dollar if it continues to climb, dealers said.

A series of official statements following Saturday's meeting of leaders of the Group of Seven industrial nations in Berlin strongly hinted they would like to see the dollar stabilize near current levels.
"Now the market is inviting intervention, except that the G7 are less apt to sell the dollar at 1.68 marks than they are at 124 yen and higher," Nelson said.
In other trade, the dollar rose to Canadian $1.3557/62 from C$1.3535/40. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7579/84 from $0.7608/13.
(( --Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664 ))
